issues.legal_issue: A purchase funded by one person but titled in another person's name is benami only when the person who supplied the purchase money intended that the titleholder should not receive the beneficial interest.
material_facts: The deceased purchaser paid the purchase price from his own funds, and the evidence did not establish that either the plaintiffs or the defendant had supplied the money.

The title document was issued in the plaintiffs’ names at the deceased purchaser’s request; the deceased later gave the document to the younger plaintiff and made statements that the house belonged to him.
The younger plaintiff and his brother had lived with the deceased, who was a bachelor; the younger plaintiff was a child when the title document was issued.

The defendant did not establish the alleged political or other reason for placing title in the plaintiffs’ names, and the deceased had no apparent need to conceal his ownership from the government selling the house.
The deceased’s conduct and statements, considered with the parties’ relationship and circumstances, showed that he intended the younger plaintiff to own the house.
issues.conclusion: The purchase was not benami. Although the deceased paid the purchase price, he intended the younger plaintiff to become the absolute owner of the house.
issues.legal_principle: The person asserting that a transaction is benami bears the burden of proof. Where the purchase money came from someone other than the titleholder, the purchase is prima facie presumed to benefit the person who supplied the money, unless evidence shows otherwise. The decisive issue is that person's intention, assessed from the source of funds, possession and nature of the property, motive, relationship of the parties, custody of title documents, and subsequent conduct. The principle underlying this form of benami transaction is recognized in section 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. The Court relied on Meenakshi Mills, Madurai v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Madras; Mohammad Sadiq Ali Khan v. Fakhr Jahan Begum; Manmohan Das v. Ramdei; and Jaydayal Poddar v. Bibi Hazra.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and purchase_money_supplied_by_someone_other_than_titleholder and title_document_names_claimant and (purchaser_delivered_title_document_to_claimant or purchaser_declared_claimant_owner) and not evidence_of_intent_to_withhold_benefit

predicates.property_title_dispute: The parties disputed who beneficially owned property acquired through a purchase.
predicates.purchase_money_supplied_by_someone_other: A person other than the person named in the title document supplied the purchase money.
predicates.title_document_names_claimant: The title document named the person claiming beneficial ownership.
predicates.purchaser_delivered_title_document_to_cl: The purchaser later delivered the title document to the claimant.
predicates.purchaser_declared_claimant_owner: The purchaser later stated that the property belonged to the claimant.
predicates.evidence_of_intent_to_withhold_benefit: Evidence showed that the purchaser intended the named titleholder not to receive the beneficial interest.

issues.definition: When a property-title dispute involves a purchase funded by someone other than the named titleholder, the named claimant is treated as beneficial owner if the title document names that claimant, the purchaser's delivery or declarations support the claimant's ownership, and there is no evidence that the purchaser intended to withhold the benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A deceased purchaser’s post-purchase statements against his proprietary interest may be admitted to prove his intention concerning the beneficial ownership of property.
material_facts: Several witnesses testified that the deceased said the disputed house belonged to the younger plaintiff and that he intended to leave his property to him.
The statements were made after the purchase and were against the deceased’s own proprietary interest.
The defendant, who stood to claim an interest if the house formed part of the deceased’s estate, disputed the use of those statements.
issues.conclusion: The deceased’s statements were admissible against his legal representative as evidence of the deceased’s intention that the younger plaintiff should own the house.
issues.legal_principle: The declarations were admissible as statements against proprietary interest under sections 21 and 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act. The Court distinguished Shephard v. Cartwright: the declarations were used against the deceased’s legal representative, not in the deceased’s favour, and the rule stated there allowed subsequent declarations as evidence against their maker.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The parties disputed who beneficially owned purchased property.
predicates.deceased_purchaser_made_post_purchase_st: The purchaser made a statement about ownership after completing the purchase.
predicates.statement_was_against_purchasers_proprie: The statement was contrary to the purchaser's own proprietary interest.
predicates.statement_is_used_against_estate_represe: A party relied on the statement against the purchaser's legal representative.

issues.definition: A deceased purchaser's post-purchase statement is admissible against the purchaser's estate when it concerns a property-title dispute, is contrary to the purchaser's proprietary interest, and is relied on against the estate's representative.

issues.legal_issue: A party may obtain relief on a proven ground that was not expressly pleaded when the issue was understood and tried by both sides without surprise.
material_facts: The plaintiffs based their claim on title documents and tried to show that they had supplied the purchase money.
The defendant pleaded that the plaintiffs were benamidars and that the real ownership lay elsewhere.
The parties knew during the trial that the character of the transaction and the intention behind putting title in the plaintiffs’ names were in dispute, and they led evidence on those matters.
The defendant had not raised before the High Court an objection that the court could not consider whether the transaction was benami.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not barred from claiming the house on the basis that the deceased purchaser intended the younger plaintiff to own it, despite their unsuccessful attempt to prove that they had supplied the purchase money.
issues.legal_principle: The general rule is that relief should rest on the pleadings, but a ground may be relied on if it is covered by an issue expressly or by implication, both sides knew it was involved in the trial, and evidence was led on it. The Court applied Bhagwati Prasad v. Shri Chandramaul, distinguished Trojan & Co. Ltd. v. R.M.N.N. Haggappa Chettiar, and referred to Ismail Mussajee Mookerdum v. Hafiz Boo.

rule.if: property_title_suit and alternative_title_ground_not_expressly_pleaded and both_sides_understood_ground_was_in_issue and both_sides_led_evidence_on_ground and no_trial_surprise

predicates.property_title_suit: The proceeding sought relief based on disputed property ownership.
predicates.alternative_title_ground_not_expressly_p: The party seeking relief did not expressly plead the ground on which the court ultimately relied.
predicates.both_sides_understood_ground_was_in_issu: Both sides understood during the proceeding that the ground was in dispute.
predicates.both_sides_led_evidence_on_ground: Both sides presented evidence bearing on the ground.
predicates.no_trial_surprise: Considering the ground did not take either side by surprise.

issues.definition: In a property-title suit, relief may be granted on a proven ground that was not expressly pleaded if both sides understood it was in issue, presented evidence on it, and were not taken by surprise.

issues.legal_issue: An occupant’s expenditure on repairs or reconstruction does not create proprietary ownership when the occupant knew the true state of title.
material_facts: The defendant argued that he had spent money on repairs and reconstruction after the title document was issued.
The Court found that the defendant had not established that he spent money on that work.
The Court added that even if he had spent money, expenditure with knowledge of the actual state of ownership would not confer a proprietary interest.
issues.conclusion: The defendant acquired no proprietary interest through the alleged expenditure, which was not proved in any event.
issues.legal_principle: Expenditure on repairs or reconstruction, even if proved, does not itself confer a proprietary interest where it is made with knowledge of the true state of ownership.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The parties disputed ownership of property occupied by one of them.
predicates.occupant_spent_money_on_repairs_or_recon: The occupant spent money repairing or reconstructing the property.
predicates.occupant_knew_true_ownership: The occupant knew who owned the property when the expenditure was made.

issues.definition: In a property-title dispute, an occupant who spends money on repairs or reconstruction while knowing the true ownership does not acquire a proprietary interest through that expenditure.

issues.legal_issue: A successful claim for possession may include mesne profits for past and continuing occupation, with future profits determined through an inquiry.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of a house and damages for its use and occupation.
The High Court stayed the trial court’s decree while the appeal was pending, and the defendant remained in possession.
By the time the Supreme Court decided the appeals, nearly twenty years had passed from the institution of the suit.
The Supreme Court ordered mesne profits for the period up to its judgment and directed the trial court to inquire into future mesne profits until possession was delivered.
issues.conclusion: The defendant was ordered to pay mesne profits for past occupation, and the trial court was directed to determine future mesne profits until delivery of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 20, Rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may direct an inquiry to determine mesne profits after judgment until delivery of possession. Given the prolonged occupation while the decree was stayed, the Court ordered past mesne profits and directed an inquiry into future profits.

rule.if: suit_for_possession and claimant_entitled_to_possession and defendant_remained_in_occupation_during_appeal and prolonged_delay_before_final_decision

predicates.suit_for_possession: The proceeding sought recovery of possession of property.
predicates.claimant_entitled_to_possession: The court determined that the claimant was entitled to possession.
predicates.defendant_remained_in_occupation_during_: The defendant continued to occupy the property while an appeal was pending.
predicates.prolonged_delay_before_final_decision: A substantial period of occupation passed before the final decision.

issues.definition: When a claimant is entitled to possession and the defendant remains in occupation through a prolonged appeal, the defendant is liable for mesne profits for past occupation and for future occupation until possession is delivered.
